one_liner: Go prefix-code varint for uint64; about 2x faster than encoding/binary Uvarint for values above 35 bits.
what_it_does: Encodes and decodes a single uint64 as a 1-9 byte prefix-code varint: the count of leading 1 bits in the first byte gives the number of extra bytes, and the value follows in big-endian order. The API mirrors encoding/binary: Encode(b []byte, v uint64) int and Decode(b []byte) (uint64, int), both returning 0 bytes instead of panicking when the slice is too short. The wire format is not LEB128, so it cannot read data written by PutUvarint, protobuf or other LEB128 producers.
how_it_is_fast: Length is known from the first byte, so decoding is one switch on the header byte followed by straight-line shifts and ORs with no per-byte continuation loop (unlike LEB128's 7-bit groups). Encoding picks the length with a range switch, ORs in the header bits and byte-swaps with math/bits.ReverseBytes16/32/64 before storing bytes. Values below 128 take an inlinable fast path in Encode; Decode is not inlined.
when_to_use: Go code that defines its own binary format and stores many uint64 values above about 2^35 (timestamps in ns, 64-bit ids, hashes), where encode drops from 5.05 to 2.99 ns and decode from 5.51 to 2.75 ns at 63 bits on an i5-11400.
Read-mostly formats where a 9-byte maximum (versus 10 for LEB128) and a length readable from the first byte are useful, for example to skip fields without decoding.
Callers that want non-panicking encode/decode with a 0-length error signal instead of binary.PutUvarint's panic on short buffers.
As a reference design for a prefix varint in C or C++; the 150-line source is BSD-3-Clause and straightforward to port.
when_not_to_use: Data that must interoperate with LEB128 (protobuf, Go encoding/binary Uvarint, DWARF, WebAssembly): the byte layout differs.
Mostly small values: at 7 bits decode is slower than binary.Uvarint (1.154 versus 0.9654 ns) and encode at 14-35 bits is level or slightly slower, so the gain exists only above about 35 bits.
Bulk integer arrays: it handles one value per call with no SIMD; block codecs such as Stream VByte or FastPFor in the catalogue are orders of magnitude faster per integer.
Signed integers: no zigzag helper is provided, only uint64.
Projects that need an active upstream: 12 commits, last one 2023-10-07, no releases.

integration.dependencies: none (math/bits from the Go standard library)
integration.platforms: any Go target; pure Go, no assembly
integration.thread_safety: Encode and Decode are pure functions with no shared state; safe for concurrent use on distinct buffers.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same call shape as binary.PutUvarint/Uvarint (with different error semantics), but an incompatible wire format, so only for new data

gotchas: The README's decoding example is wrong: it calls varint.Decod and binds the results as 'l, v', while Decode returns (value, length); copying it will not compile and, once fixed, swaps the variables.

Decode accepts non-minimal encodings (for example 0x80 0x05 decodes to 5), so the same value can have several byte representations; do not hash or compare encoded bytes for equality without re-encoding.

The benchmark encodes one constant value per sub-benchmark (always the same branch), which the README itself says favours this code; and it uses a buffer whose length is rand.Int()%1010, so a run with a length under 9 would make Encode a silent no-op.
Tests check one bit pattern (0xAAAA...) per width plus the empty buffer; there is no fuzzing or truncated-value test beyond length 0.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over dennwc/varint when you control the format and your values are mostly large (dennwc keeps LEB128 compatibility and gains at small sizes too); choose streamvbyte-simdgo or Stream VByte for arrays of 32-bit values rather than one-off uint64 fields.
verified_claims_summary: First-party go test -bench output on an 11th Gen Intel Core i5-11400 (Linux amd64, Go version not stated) compares Encode/Decode with binary.PutUvarint/Uvarint, one fixed value per bit width: at 63 bits encode is 2.992 versus 5.051 ns/op and decode 2.754 versus 5.510 ns/op (about 1.7x and 2.0x, derived from page data); at 7 bits encode ties and decode is about 20% slower.
status_note: Stale since 2023-10-07 (15 stars, no open issues, no releases), but BSD-3-Clause and a single small file, so easy to vendor or port.
